item.title: 1. Introduction
item.description:
Introduction

NONMEM

NONMEM stands for "Nonlinear Mixed Effects Model." Written in Fortran 90/95, NONMEM fits general nonlinear regression-type models to data. The data are typically collected from clinical studies of pharmaceutic agents, involving the administration of a drug to individuals and the subsequent observation of drug levels (most often in the blood plasma). Proper modeling of these data involves accounting for both inter- and intra-subject effects (random effects), as well as measured concomitant effects (fixed effects). This mixed effect modeling approach, and the nonlinear nature of the biochemical and physiological process involved, is the bedrock of NONMEM. Such modeling is especially useful when there are only a few pharmacokinetic measurements from each individual sampled in the population, or when the data collection design varies considerably between these individuals. However, NONMEM is a general program which can be used to fit models to a wide variety of data.

item.title: 2. Population models
item.description:
Population models

In this chapter we discuss models for populations data. Those data contain observations from a set of individuals sampled from a population. Such data are characterized by one or more observations for each individual. All the models discussed here are parameter models, in that observations are described with models with parameters. These models are capable of explaining the data variability due to the those unknown random parameters.

item.title: 3. Model fitting
item.description:
Model fitting

All fitting methods aim to adjust model parameters so that model predictions match the observed data in an 'optimal' way. This set of "optimal" parameter values is called the parameter estimates. We use \(\hat{\theta}\), \(\hat{\Omega}\), and \(\hat{\Sigma}\) to denote estimates to the correspoding NONMEM parameters. Different methods define “optimal” in different ways. For example, NONMEM's classical methods such as FO use a least-squares type criterion, the exact form of which depends on the chosen error model.
